Safety of the goods carried by the Railways 
*41. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that goods carried by the Railways which was over 88 per cent 
in 1970s have come down to merely 40 per cent in late 1990s; 
(b) if so, how far lack of safety of ca rriages, pilferage of goods spreading 
corruption and ill-maintenance of rail-wagons and other equipments are responsible 
for the less earnings of the Railways from goods and freight; and 
(c) what additional safety measures and other steps including raids are being 
taken by Government this year? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. In the year 1970-71, the Railways carried 69 percent of goods 
traffic which came down to around 40 per cent in the year 1995-96. 
(b) No, Sir. On the contrary, number of claims for compensation for loss, damage, 
deficiency, deterioration of goods have significantly reduced and proper maintenance of 
wagons is being ensured. 
(c) Checks to prevent claims, pilferages, overloading etc. are being conducted on 
regular basis.

(a) to (c) The New Pricing Scheme (NPS) for urea units was introduced 
w.e.f. 1.4.2003 replacing the erstwhile Retention Price Scheme. NPS is being 
implemented in stages. Stage-I was of one year duration effective from 
1.4.2003 to 31.3.2004 and Stage-ll is of two year duration commencing from 
1.4.2004 and will be up to 31.3.2006. While communicating the salient 
features of the NPS, it was laid down that the modalities of Stage-Ill would be 
decided by the Department of Fer tilizers (DoF) after review of the 
implementation of Stage-I and Stage-ll. 
In compliance of this, a Working Group is proposed to be constituted, which 
will apart from, reviewing th e effectiveness of Stage-I' and II of NPS and for 
formulating policy for urea units beyond for Stage-Ill commencing from 
1.4.2006, would also examine issues pertaining to formulation of feedstock 
policy especially with regard to nature; pricing and availability, demand and 
supply of urea upto the end of Eleventh Five Year Plan, fixing milestones for 
conversion of existing naphtha and FO/LSHS based units to NG/LNG, mode 
of determination and methodology of payment of concession to urea units, 
decontrol of movement and distribution of urea, balanced fertilization through 
urea pricing etc.

*46. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will th e Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many cases of illegal transplant of kidney in 
Government and private hospitals have come to light during current year; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the action taken against the erring doctors, middlemen and hospitals; 
and 
(d) whether there is a provision in the law to compensate the innocent donor 
duped into parting with a kidney, for a minimum six figure amount in rupees, 
from out of the fines/penalties levied on the doctors/hospitals? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE 
(DR.ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2004] 
Statement 
Recently, five cases of alleged illegal transplant of kidneys in hospitals located 
in Delhi have come to the notice of the Government of India. In this connection, 
Delhi Police has registered a number of  FIRs against Research and Referral 
Hospital, New Delhi; Indraprasth Apollo Hospital, New Delhi; and Sir Ganga 
Ram Hospital, New Delhi. As a result, ten people have been arrested by the Delhi 
Police. The cases are currently under investigation by the Delhi Police. One case has 
also been reported from Maharashtra in respect of Bombay Hospital and Research 
Centre, Mumbai. 
Sale and purchase of human organs, including kidney, is banned under 
the provisions of the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994. The Act 
contains stringent povisions for punishing any one who commits such offences. 
Under Section 13 of the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994, the Central 
and State Governments are empowered to appoint Appropriate Authorities for the 
purpose of the Act who are empowered to investigate any complaints of breach 
of provisions of the Act including those pertaining to sale and purchase of 
human organs, including kidney. The Director-General of Health Services is the 
Appopriate Authority appointed by the Central Government in respect of 
Union Territories including the National Capital Territory of Delhi. 
There is no provision under the said Act to compensate the victims of 
commercial dealings in human organs from out of the fines or penalties levied on 
the doctors or hospitals registered under the Act. However, a Committee has 
been constituted in September, 2004 under directions of Delhi High Court in 
Case No. WP(C) 813/2004 to look into various aspects relating to transplantation 
of human organs and to suggest corrective measures. The Committee has been 
asked to give its report by January, 2005.

Water cess on sea water 
*50.  PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA:† 
SHRI ABANI ROY: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that sea water is available in the country in 
abundance; 
(b) whether Government have issued notification for collection of cess on use of 
sea water by State Pollution Authorities; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the reasons for collecting cess on sea water and 
how much revenue is likely to be collected by Government; 
(d) whether imposing of cess on sea water will hamper the industrial growth in the 
country especially in and around coastal areas; and 
(e) if so, the steps being taken to withdraw cess on sea water? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) 
to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 provides 
for the levy of a cess on industries and local bodies using water. There is no separate 
notification regarding levy of cess on use of sea water. The cess is intended to minimize 
consumption and pollution of water by the industries and local authorities. The cess amount 
is utilized for augmenting the resources of the Central and State Pollution Control Boards. 
Every person carrying on any industry and every local authority using water, irrespective 
of the source from where water is drawn, is liable to pay cess based on the quantity of 
water consumed by them. The water cess is collected by the Governments of States and 
Union Territories from all the industries, except Hydel Power Units, and is remitted to the 
Consolidated Fund of India every month in lump sum. No separate account is maintained about 
the cess collected from the industries using sea water.

year 2003-04 was Rs.88.50 crores.

including sea water have to bear for the protection of the environment and 
conservation of natural resources.

*52. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the prime cause of stampede and resultant deaths at 
29 

RAJYA SABHA                 [3 December, 2004] 
New Delhi Railway Station recently was due to issuing of unreserved tickets to destinations 
in Bihar much beyond the capacity; 
(b) whether to derive more revenue Railways permit unreserved passengers to 
travel in reserved sleeper coaches much beyond capacity causing inconvenience and 
harassment to reserved passengers; and 
(c) what steps are being proposed to lessen the crowd on platforms including 
curtailment of persons accompanying travellers within station premises? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. 
VELU): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. The incident could only be taken as an unfortunate isolated incident and 
there was no lapse on anybody's part which would have caused the lady passenger to fall. 
The enquiry committee after examining eye witnesses held no one responsible for the 
incident. 
On 13.11.2004 Train No.2388 Down Jan Sadharan Express scheduled to start 
at 1510 hrs. was placed at Platform No.3 at 1100 hrs., and the doors were opened at 1210 
hrs. There was heavy rush at New Delhi Railway Station due to Chhat Festival and Id 
towards Bihar. While crowd was descending to Platform No. 3 to board Jan Sadharan 
Express, suddenly an elderly woman, due to pressure of rush, slipped down on the 
landing of Foot Over Bridge of Platform No. 2/3. Consequently, some more passengers 
panicked and a stampede started which resulted in stumbling of some more 
passengers. 
5 ladies, including one 14 years old girl, unfortunately, succumbed to their injuries. Of 
the remaining 10 injured, 2 who were having convulsions were shifted to Ram Manohar 
Lohia Hospital. All the others were provided proper treatment at Northern Railway Central 
Hospital. One doctor was specially deputed at Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital to look after 
the injured and all the medicines were made available for the injured admitted in Ram 
Manohar Lohia Hospital. 
Unreserved tickets are not issued fo r any specific train. The unreserved 
tickets are issued only for a particular destination in the second

unreserved tickets cannot be linked to carrying capacity of a specific train. 
(b) Railways, as a policy, do not permit unreserved passengers to travel in 
reserved sleeper glass coaches, as the unreserved tickets are not valid for travel in 
reserved coaches. 
(c) It is proposed to review the platform ticket policy. Public will also be educated to 
avoid congestion at Railway Stations. Accordingly, in order to prevent future recurrence of 
such incidents of overcrowding, it is proposed to install Closed Circuit Television 
System (CCTV); speeding of the construction of sanctioned buildings and terminals 
besides Foot Over Bridges.

as an alternative urban transportation device to underground metros and over 
land rail tracks? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Trial runs en the test track commenced from 25th August, 2004. On a 
return trip, during trial runs on 25th September, 2004, the Officer in-charge 
observed that the Sky Bus speed wa s not getting controlled as it was 
approaching the curve ahead of stopping point, and since the speed was restricted 
to 20 Kmph on the curve, at some distance in advance of the approach of curve, 
he reacted to take action to abort the experiment by pressing the emergency 
button. This provides for cutting off the power and application of pneumatic 
breaks. The officer did not immediately feel

Kernex Microsystems India Ltd. and Ramchandra Murthy, AC Mechanic, South Western 
Railway were injured. 
An enquiry by a Committee consisting of four Heads of the Department of Konkan 
Railway assisted by Prof. S.C. Lakkad, Deputy Director of Indian Institute of 
Technology, Pawai and Austrian Engineer has been ordered by Managing Director,

feasibility of establishing and operating Sky Bus metro service in Indian cities. The 
terms of reference of this Committee are as under: 
(i) To examine the tech no-economic and financial feasibility of the Sky Bus 
metro system. 
(ii) To ascertain the safety of the system. 
(iii) To critically evaluate novel system component, such as suspended 
rail technology, traversing systems, etc. 
(iv) To critically evaluate the integration of different technologies. 
(v) Any other matter considered relevant by the Committee.

THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. On 
13.11.2004, Train No. 2388 Dn. Jan Sadharan Exp. scheduled to start at 1510 hrs. was placed 
at Platform No. 3 at 1100 hrs., and the doors were opened at 1210 hrs. There was heavy 
rush at New Delhi Railway Station due to Chhat Festival and Id towards Bihar. While 
crowd was descending to Platform No. 3 to board Jan Sadharan Express, suddenly an 
elderly woman, due to pressure of rush, slipped down on the landing of Foot Over Bridge 
of Platform No. 2/3. Consequently, some more passengers panicked and a stampede 
started which resulted in stumbling of some more passengers. 
5 ladies, including one 14 years old girl unfortunately, succumbed to their injuries. Of 
the remaining 10 injured, 2 who were having convulsions were shifted to Ram Manohar 
Lohia Hospital. All the others were provided proper treatment at Northern Railway Central 
Hospital. One doctor was specially deputed at Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital to look after 
the injured and all the medicines were made available for the injured admitted in Ram 
Manohar Lohia Hospital. 
(c) and (d) A fact-finding enquiry was ordered by the General Manager/ Northern 
Railway by a committee consisting of Chief Traffic Manager, Deputy Commissioner of 
Police (Crime & Railways), Addl. Chief Security Commissioner/Railway Protection Force 
and Additional Divisional Railway Manager (Operations) Delhi. 
The enquiry by the above Committee revealed that the incident could only be taken as 
an unfortunate isolated incident and there was no lapse on anybody's part which would 
have caused the lady passenger to fall. Therefore, the Committee held no one responsible 
for the incident.

stampede:—

Special Trains from alternative stations.

Statement 
Details of modalities evolved to improve agricultural credit flow and farm 
produce prices 
A. AGRICULTURAL CREDIT 
Pursuant to the announcement made by the Finance Minister on 18th June, 
2004 containing measures for improving agricultural credit flow and providing 
credit related relief to farmers, the banks have been ' advised as under: 
I. Total flow of agricultural credit which is estimated at Rs. 80,000 crore 
in 2003-04 will be enhanced to about Rs. 105,000 crore in 2004-05. 
This will represent a 30 per cent increase over the flow of credit in 
the previous year. 
53 

RAJYA SABHA         [3 December, 2004] 
II. Every effort will be made to enhance coverage of institutional 
credit, including through KCCs, in line with the higher goal for 
agricultural credit in 2004-05. 
III. Commercial banks will make an effort to bring into their fold, on 
average, at least 100 new farmers at each rural and semi-rural branch 
during the current year. The goal is  to enlarge the Universe of new 
farmers borrowing from banks by about 50 lakh. 
IV. Each rural and semi-urban branch of commercial banks will take 
up at least two to three new investment projects in the area of 
plantation and horticulture, fisheries, organic farming, agro-
processing, live stock, micro-irrigation, sprinkler irrigation, 
watershed management, village  ponds development and other 
agricultural activities. 
V In every district, all commercial banks put together will finance 10 
agro-clinics during the current year. 
VI. In order to provide credit to tenant farmers and oral lessees, 
NABARD will facilitate formation and financing of self-help 
groups of tenant farmers and oral lessees' during the- current year. 
VII. Scales of finance will be reviewed to meet the realistic credit needs 
of farmers, especially capital intensive agricultural operations. 
VIII. Debt restructuring will be done by the commercial banks, RRBs and 
cooperatives under the following heads in accordance with the new 
guidelines issued by RBI/NABARD: 
• Farmers in distress—Debts of farmers as on 31st March, 2004 in 
disricts declared as calamity-a ffected by the State Government 
concerned will be rescheduled/restructured. Interest outstanding 
in the accounts of such borrowers will be clubbed with the 
principal outstanding on March 31,2004, and the am ount thus 
arrived at shall be repayable over a period of five years, at 
current interest rates, including an initial moratorium of two 
years. 
54 

[3 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
• Farmers in arrears—Loans in default of farmers who have 
become ineligible for fresh credit as their earlier debts have 
been categorized as sub-standard or doubtful will be 
rescheduled as per the guidelines issued by NABARD/RBI 
so that such farmers become eligible for fresh credit. 
 OTS for small and marginal farmers—Guidelines for 
increasing the flexibility of banks and cooperatives to grant 
a one-time settlement (OTS) for small and marginal farmers 
who have been declared as defaulters and have become 
ineligible for fresh credit from lending institutions will be issued 
by RBI/NABARD. Management of banks and cooperatives 
will be advised to review case s where credit has been denied 
on the sole ground that a loan account was settled through 
compromise or write offs. 
• In some parts of the countr y, farmers face acute distress 
because of the heavy burden of debt from non-institutional 
lenders (e.g., moneylenders).  Banks have been permitted

Reforms in agriculture sector 
193. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to introduce reforms in the agriculture sector 
with the intention to step up investments and remove untoward controls in 
farming; 
(b) if so, by when they are to be introduced alongwith the complete details 
thereof; and 
(c) in what manner the proposed reforms in the agriculture sector would 
help the overall performance of the farm sector in terms of investment, 
marketing and production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Agriculture sector needs well functioning markets to drive growth, 
employment and economic prosperity in rural areas of the country. In order to 
provide dynamism and efficiency into the marketing system, large 
investments are required for the development of post harvest and cold chain 
infrastructure near to the farmers' field. Projection of production and marketable 
surplus of various farm products was recently assessed by an Expert Committee 
set up by the Ministry of Agriculture which estimated that an investment 
requirement of Rs. 11,142 crore in next 10 years would be necessary for 
infrastructure development for agricultural marketing. A major portion of this 
investment is expected from the private sector, for which an appropriate 
regulatory and policy environment is necessary. 
The Ministry is well on this path of reform and has had several rounds of 
discussion with the States including restrictive provisions of State Law in 
Agricultural Marketing (APMC Act) which hamper effective transmission of 
market signals, and thereby the need to modify and create lawful space for the 
private sector in market development and contract farming. 
56 

 [3 December, 2004]              RAJYA SABHA 
Alongside, enabling policies have also  to be put in place to encourage 
procurement of agricultural commodities directly from farmers' field, 
establishment of effective linkage between farm production and the retail chain, 
including food processing industries. Promotion of direct marketing, contract 
farming and development of competitive agricultural markets in private and 
cooperative sectors have been identified as key areas of reform, inter-alia, 
requiring amendments to the State APMC Act. 
In order to guide the State in implementation of the suggested reforms, the 
Ministry of Agriculture has formulat ed a Model State Agricultural Produce 
Marketing (Development and Regulation) Act and circulated to all the State 
Governments/UT Administrations for further necessary action as the subject 
matter falls within their purview. The aforesaid reforms in the Model Law were 
discussed in a meeting of State Agriculture Ministers held on 19th November, 
2004. All the States/UTs have been requested to suitably amend their APMC Act 
in the overall national/State interest and more so in the interest of farmers. 
With a view to attract large investments for development of agriculture 
markets in the country, this Ministry has approved a new reform linked 
scheme under which assistance would be provided to the States, who amends 
the APMC Act to promote direct marketing, contract farming and competitive 
markets in private and cooperative sectors. The scheme will be implemented 
during Tenth Plan with an outlay of Rs. 190 crore for providing subsidy @ 25 
per cent of the capital investment and @ 33.33 per cent for NE, hilly and tribal 
areas and to SC/ST entrepreneurs. 
(c) The implementation of the proposed reforms would enable the private 
and cooperative sectors to make investment in setting up of markets, direct 
procurement of agricultural commodities from farmers' fields by the food 
processing industries and retail chains. Once these effective linkages between 
farm production, processing industries and retail chain are established, this 
would enable a higher share for the farmers in the price of his agricultural 
produce.

Supreme Court of India has held that the legal position is almost firmly 
established that where a patient dies due to the negligent medical treatment of the 
doctor, the doctor can be made liable in civil law for paying compensation and 
damages in tort and at the same time, if the degree of negligence is so gross and 
his act was so reckless as to endanger the life of the patient, he would also be 
made criminally liable for offence under Section 304-A IPC. For fixing criminal 
liability on a doctor or surgeon, the standard of negligence required to be proved 
should be so high as can be described as "gross negligence" or "recklessness". It 
further held that mere inadvertence or some degree of want of adequate care and 
caution might create civil liability but would not suffice to hold him criminally 
liable. In this case, the Hon'ble Court finally held that no case of recklessness or 
gross negligence had been made out against the doctor concerned to compel 
him to face trial for offence under Section 304-A of IPC. 
At present, the Central Government has no proposal to prefer a review 
petition against the above judgement of the Supreme Court. There are provisions 
available in the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and 
Ethics) Regulations 2002 under which any complaint with regard to 
professional misconduct ag ainst a doctor can be brought before the Medical 
Council of India or appropriate State Medical Council and if the concerned Council 
after holding an enquiry in the matter comes to the conclusion that the doctor 
concerned is guilty of misconduct, the Council may award such punishment as 
deem necessary or may direct removal altogether or for a specified period, the 
name of the delinquent doctor from the Register.

SHRI TARIQANWAR:

[3 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof;

investigate the matter in view of its seriousness; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKALAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Based 
on the news report which appeared in the National Newspapers in India on 28th 
September, 2004, the matter was taken up with British High Commission in 
order to confirm the supply of blood product suspected to be contaminated with 
human form of mad cow disease. The enquiry reveals that 22 vials of vigam-
S 5g (Human Normal Immunologlobulin) batch No. VGC 085 manufactured 
by M/s Bio Products Laboratory, U.K. was exported to India and the blood 
donor who donated source plasma later development vCJD. M/s Bio Products 
Laboratory, U.K. has informed that they have exported this consignment to M/s 
Genexx Chemicals Pvt. Ltd., New Delhi in 1997. The said lot was 
manufactured in July, '97 and hence the expiry date was August, '99. 
(c) and (d) After enquiry into the matter, British High Commission has 
clarified that the estimated level of ineffectivity for any patient is judged 
according to the new U.K. critieria of having passed the "at risk" threshold and 
need for only public health precautions. 
As per information available from WHO and European Medicine 
Agency, there is no credible instance of transmission of CJD through blood 
products. National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS) 
Bangalore has also informed that no case of CJD is reported from India till date. 
Further on enquiry, it has been clarified that the blood product manufacturers in 
U.K. are using imported plasma from USA since 1998 to manufacture the blood 
products in order to avoid the risk of vCJD problem. So far, Government has 
not received any reported incidence of vCJD disease through blood products in 
the country.

263.   SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: 
DR. PRABHATHAKUR: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state; 
(a) whether it is a fact that instances of circulation of spurious drugs have

124 

[3 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so,,the details of complaints re gistered by affected consumers with 
the authorities and sources of circulations  uncovered, if any, by enforcement 
agencies, year-wise, during the last five years; 
(c) whether any survey has been carried out by Government with a view to 
ascertain the spurious drug menace in all its dimensions; 
(d) if so, the finding thereof; 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(f) what were the salient observations and recommendations made in 2003 
by the Committee headed by R.A. Mashelkar, DG, CSIR, in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKALAKSHMI): (a) There have 
been media reports quoting varying figures about the alleged extent of 
circulation of spurious drugs in the country. However, as per the feedback 
available from the Drugs Controllers of States/UTs, 36947,38824, 36314, 39465 
drugs samples were tested during the period 2000-01, 2001-02, 2002-03 and 
2003-04, out of which 112, 96, 125 and 108 samples respectively were found 
spurious which is 0.3, 0.25, 0.34 and 0.27% of the samples tested. Thus it does 
not appear that the spurious medicines have been growing alarmingly. 
(b) Action against any complaints for possible manufacture or sale of 
spurious drugs is taken by State Governments through their respective drugs 
control organizations. In view of this, specific details of the complaints 
registered by consumers with the drugs control authorities of States/UTs are not 
maintained Centrally. However, Government of India has been taking various 
initiatives to ensure uniform and strict action to tackle the problem of spurious 
drugs. Some of such specific initiatives are as follows:— 
(i) Issues concerning alleged sale of spurious drugs taken up by Union 
Health Minister with State Health  Ministers in the conference of 
Central Council of Health and Family Welfare. 
(ii) Meeting of State Drug Controllers together with representatives of 
pharma industry and trade organizations, arranged. 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2004] 
(iii) Financial assistance provided to States for augmentation of drug testing 
facilities. 
(iv) Matter concerning sale of spurious drugs and initiatives to be taken 
up by State Governments were taken up by Union Health Minister 
with all Chief Ministers in October, 2002. 
(v) A World Bank assisted Capacity Building Project on Food Safety and 
Quality Control of Drugs has been launched with effect from 
October, 2003. This project aims at strengthening, inter-alia, the 
drug regulatory infrastructure in the country by augmenting the 
drug testing facilities by providing for equipments, civil works, 
staff and consumables and extensive training of drugs 
regulatory/quality control officials and industry personnel. Annual 
drug testing capacity to be raised to 1,00,000 samples as against 
36,000 to 38,000 samples. 
(vi) Special training programme for improving investigations and legal 
skills organized for State officials. 
(c) to (e) Manufacture of spurious  drugs is primarily a clandestine 
activity. Being a clandestine activity, it is difficult to assess the actual 
quantum of spurious drugs. However, a study of samples of drugs tested all over 
the country in last 4 to 5 years, reveals that about 0.2% to 0.3% of samples fall 
within the category of spurious drugs. 
(f) Based on the recommendations of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar Committee, a 
legislation to amend the penal provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, 
and to provide for stricter penalties to the offenders including a maximum 
penalty of capital punishments, was introduced in the Parliament in 
December, 2003. 
The salient amendments proposed under the Bill are given below:— 
1. Enhance the punishment relating to spurious or adulterated drugs 
leading to death or grievous hurt within the meaning of Section 320 
IPC upto punishment of death or imprisonment for a term which 
shall not be less than 10 years but which may extend to 
imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fined of one lakh 
rupees or upto three times the value of the goods seized, whichever 
is higher. 
126 

[3 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
2. Penalities for subsequent offences to be enhanced upto 10 years 
and with fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees. 
3. Offences relating to spurious or adulterated drugs to be made non-
bailable and cognizable. 
4. Provision for setting up of special courts to try offences or 
spurious or adulterated drugs. 
5. To confer powers upon police offices not below the rank of sub-
inspector or other designated officers to institute prosecutions under 
the said Act. 
6. Provision for compounding of offences for minor offences under the 
Act. 
The proposed amendments will make the Law deterrent to the offenders 
involved in the manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The involvement of 
enforcing agencies like Police will help in speedy investigations to book the 
culprits and in controlling anti-social elements involved in such activities. 
Since the Bill has now lapsed with the dissolution of previous Lok Sabha, 
necessary action to introduce a bill to enhance penalties for manufacture 
and/or sale of spurious and/or adulterated drugs under the Drugs & Cosmetics 
Act, 1940, has been initiated by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.

275.   PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: SHRI 
MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the popular pain killer Rofecoxib has 
recently been banned in the United States; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it has also been banned in our country by Government on the 
recommendation of an Expert Group; 
(d) if so, the names of the companies who were manufacturing this medicine; 
(e) whether Government are aware that this medicine is still available in the shops; 
and 
(f) if so,  the steps being taken against those selling this banned drug? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
140 

[3 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) and (c) Based on the announcement made by innovator, Merck USA, 
on withdrawal of Rofecoxib worldwide on 30th September, 2004, following 
clinical trial results, which showed an increase risk of confirmed serious events 
(including myocardial infraction and stroke) compared to placebo, following 
long-term use, and based on available published literature, expert group in 
India recommended withdrawal of Rofecoxib formulations. 
(d) The names of the major companies who were manufacturing this 
medicine are: M/s. Ranbaxy Lab., Unichem, Lupin, Torrent Pharma, Sun 
Pharma, Micro Lab., Dr. Reddy's Lab. etc. 
(e) and (f) Notification with regard to  ban of Rofecoxib formulations 
under section 26Aof Drug and Cosmetic Act is under process. Only after 
publication of said notification the drug stands banned. In the meanwhile a 
Press Note has been issued to widely publicize this.

SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT (Maharashtra) : Sir, I am raising an issue of

Need for providing telephone facility at Machil in Kupwara district of Jammu 
and Kashmir 
PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ (Jammu a nd Kashmir): Mr. Deputy Chairman, 
Sir, we must feel rightly proud of our adva ncement in the field of telecommunications 
and information technology. But, then, the 'Ministry concerned must feel duty bound 
to ensure proper communication facilities in what are called 'backward areas'. 
Recently, I visited Machil in Kupwara District of Kashmir, and, to my horror, I found 
Machil, with a population of 10,000 people,  without telephone facility. Machil 
remains, cut-off for.seven months from Kashmir valley and the plight of the people in 
the absence of any telecommunication link can be imagined. It is a tragedy that a small 
telephone exchange at Machil has not been provided all these years. 
The Department of Telecommunications has not taken any notice of the fact 
that even the Army in that area is interested that telephone facility must be provided to 
the people of Machil. I was pleasantly surpri sed when a senior Army officer in Machil 
suggested that the telephone wiring could be  provided through the poles and circuits 
that belong to the Army to make available th is most important facility to the civilian 
population. 
I strongly urge the Ministry of Te lecommunications to visit Machil and 
ensure telephone facility there. The Chief General Manager of the circle should visit 
the area immediately, and, initiate measures to ensure the facility.

Request to bring back Prisoners of War from Pakistani jails 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODiA  (Rajasthan ): Sir, after languishing in 
Pakistani Jail for long five years, two Ar my jawans, namely, Lance Naik Jagsir Singh 
and Sapper Mohammed Arif, returned home a few days back. Everyone welcomed 
their return to the motherland. They were lost and forgotten and, in fact, declared 
'deserters' whereas Pakistan has mentioned them as PoWs. 
It was surprising to note that the so ldiers were languishing in a Rawalpindi 
prison till the newspapers revealed that they were not 'deserters' but soldiers arrested 
by Pakistan for straying across the LoC near Kargil on September 17, 1999. 
Going through such conflicting reports, many questions come to our mind in 
the matter of declaring such soldiers as 'deserters' without 
183

making much efforts to find out the fact s of their disappearance in the given 
circumstances, whether thorough enquiries ar e not made during the war, or after the 
war comes to an end; or whether lists of prisoners are not exchanged with the enemy's 
commanders. In order to avoid recurrence of such instances, our Defence forces must 
make self-assessment as to why they give  up so soon in such cases. No one should 
cause unimaginable insult and humiliation to these brave soldiers and their families. 
The Government should also find out  about other missing people during the 
war or otherwise, and also about the PoWs still in the custody of Pakistan, and 
ascertain as to how fast they can be brought back home to join their near and dear 
ones.

SHRI ARUN. JAITLEY (Gujarat): Sir,  let me first of all congratulate 
Shrimati Kum Kum Rai for having introduced, as a Private Members' Bill, a very 
progressive piece of legislatio n. As Shri Jairam Ramesh wa s mentioning, over the last 
few years, ever since this campaign for equalit y in terms of property rights, equality in 
terms of various other rights, as far as wo men in our society are concerned, has been 
built up, there has been a periodic review in  the society itself. There are broadly two 
challenges before us. The first challenge is, have we kept pace with the changing times 
and updated our laws to bring about and actual ly confer the right of equality? And the 
second challenge really is, even through legislation when we are able to implement the 
principle of equality, is the social envi ronment of the society still accepting those 
legislations and implementing those legislations? Let me start with the second point 
first. It was in the late 1950s that the am endments to the Hindu laws were made. In 
those amendments, several rights of equality in terms of parental property were 
206 

[3 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
conferred upon the Hindu women. Even today,  45 years later, we still find that the 
social environment of the society has not readily implemented what has been the 
mandate of the laws made by this Parliament. I, therefore, feel that there has to be 
two-pronged attempt. One attempt, of course, is to keep the changes in the law with 
the pace that is required and the second is to  create an adequate social opinion in the 
society where social pressures to implement those laws are also increased and 
implemented. 
Sir, I have always believed and that also is the mandate of our Constitution 
in Article 13, sub-clause (2), that all laws  should conform to rights conferred by Part 
III of the Constitution, that is, the Constitu tional Guarantees. Now, when the mandate 
of the Constitution is that all laws must  conform to the constitutional guarantees, 
somehow we have kept, because of the c onstraints of our system, personal laws 
outside the ambit of those laws which are required to conform to the constitutional 
guarantees. Even judicial opinion which had a great opportunity to accept this 
principle that when all laws must conf orm to Fundamental Rights, the right to 
equality, the right of women to live with di gnity, why is it that personal laws we were 
able to keep out of the system and even judicial mandate did not so require? I think 
one of the greatest challenges for India in the years to come is going to be whether 
both the Parliamentary System and our Judicial System will bring even those laws 
within the conferment of article 13 itself and enforce the principle of equality even as 
far as those laws are concerned. Once we are able to achieve this, one of the necessary 
consequences that will follow, that we w ill be putting on the road map, the right to 
equality, the right to dignity as far as  our women are concerned. You require 
education, an educati onal standard to improve for wome n if we are to confer a sense 
of dignity to them, you require to confer a certain element of income upon them so 
that they are in a position to earn. You also require to confer the right to property, as 
far as women are concerned. Now, one of  the arguments which has been raised 
traditionally as far as the ri ght of property is concerned -a nd this is one of the reasons 
why we have been lacking in our efforts to confer this right- is that if this right is 
conferred upon women and they  get married, this will lead to bifurcation and 
trifurcation of land holdings; and, therefore, we will face resistance as far as large number 
of sections of the society are concerned. Now, we have five States* in India, four Southern 
States and the State of Maharashtra, which in relation to the Undivided Hindu Family have 
already implemented certain radical reforms. In fact, Kerala has gone a step ahead of the 
other three Southern States in implementing those reforms.   Once 
207 

RAJYA SABHA [3 December, 2004] 
those have been legislated in those five States, the kind of resistance, at times, which 
we anticipate which may be faced, certainly, was not faced in those States. But the 
second challenge which still remains is that even after having brought the legislation to 
that effect in those five States, that is, Maharashtra and four Southern States, the 
implementation process of that legislation has been somewhat slow. And, therefore, 
Sir, when Dr. Kum Kum Rai has introduced th is piece of legislation I have just two 
suggestions to offer, for the hon. Law Minist er who is present here to consider. The 
first is, one of the big problems that we had been facing in our courts of law, 
particularly, in relation to women who are not being maintained, is the absence of 
adequate standards of maintenance and the expeditious grant of them. Now, over the 
last few years, laws were changed to improve the quantum as also to provide for 
certain advisory guidelines in terms of tim eframe so that it could be implemented 
quickly. I think, it requires to be studied whether the implementation of what this 
Parliament has mandated is act ually taking place or not, or, is the process still very 
slow. 
The second factor -- and, I think, when I see the text of this legislation which 
is inbuilt in the spirit of this legislation — is how do you give a relief or a right, I don't 
even want to use the word 'relief, give a right, as far as property is concerned. Now, the 
right to property has been evolved world-ove r, in different ways. There are countries 
which jurisprudentially expounded the conc ept of the husband's house as being the 
matrimonial home. So, it really belongs to  both the wife and the husband together. 
Alternatively, in the parental  property, or, in the in-law s' property, or, the husband's 
property, or, in both, some legislative change s have to be there to ensure a mandatory 
right for women. That is, tomorrow, if she becomes a widow, tomorrow if she gets 
separated, or even if she is having a ha ppy married life, and I hope, most women do 
have that, if she is living in a husband's house,  at least, she lives there with a sense of 
dignity that 'I can't be thrown out at some body's will'. Now, once this is mandated by 
law itself, slowly, but surely -- it will take  time; that has been our experience since 
1957 - the social acceptability of this in the years is going to come. With regard to the 
question which I had raised about the refo rms which have been made in the four 
Southern States and Maharashtra, which have still not been made in the rest of the 
country, I would urge the hon. Law Minister to seriously consider referring this issue 
for some debate and maki ng a recommendation to the Law Commission itself. And, 
the reason I state is that the whole concept of family structure in India is undergoing a 
change.   Fifty years ago, the concept of larger families, joint families was 
208 

[3 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
very prevalent. With each day which is pa ssing by, this concept is getting gradually 
eroded. Now, therefore, allowing this concept to remain for the purposes of 
excluding the right of a woman in the propert y rights, I think, is a question, which on 
account of the changing socio-economic en vironment today would also require a 
reconsideration. Secondly, Sir, there are also  still some legislations which have been 
discussed in the past in the Government, in this Parliament, where changes are 
required in property laws, in succession laws, where some aberrations to the principle 
of equality still remain. For instance, even when the property is not an ancestral or an 
undivided Hindu family propert y but just a joint property in which a Hindu lady has 
a share, she may have a right but she is still prevented from enforcing a partition of 
that property and enforcing a share in it. It is only when the male members decide to 
partition it that she will get her share. Now, in the year 2004, does it or does it not 
require a reconsideration whether such a la w should remain on the statute? And, I, 
therefore, go back to where I had started from; if we now start testing each one of 
these issues on the principle of equality, on the principle of dignity, that these are the 
rights which we have to confer on a wo man, then-I don't know whether -- what.Mr. 
Nariman suggested that we should have a larger comprehensive law which deals with 
all this - that is so easily possible or not. If that were possible, all of us would be too 
happy about it. But even if that is not possible, if we can really review each one of 
these laws which still remain an aberration to  the rule of equality and think in terms 
of making a forward movement in some of  them, I think, we would be leaving a 
considerable amount of impact  as far as the right to equality and dignity for Indian 
women is concerned. 
Sir, thank you very much for givi ng me an opportunity. Let me again 
congratulate Dr. Rai for bringing this Bill.

And, those of us, who know a little bit of history of codification of laws in 
India are aware, if we go back to the Charter Act, 1833, when India was governed as 
Princely States, it was Lord Macaulay and his team of jurists from Britain, who came 
to India and gave a uniform system of laws in  India, and, a uniform system of codes in 
India. When this Act was de bated, I remember, and, I vi vidly remember the words of 
Lord Macaulay when he said, "this is a country which requires uniform laws because it 
is a country where there are different kinds of law in different parts of India". There 
were States, and, each State had its own kind of laws, and, in India, the ancient law 
was the Dharamashastra. Where there was a Hindu State, it was governed according 
to the Dharamashastra, with whatever Dharamashastra was prevalent. 
Dharamashastra was a system of administration of ju stice according to scriptures. In 
some Muslim States, you had the Muslim Personal Law as well as Muslim laws in 
those States. But, when the British felt that this country needs uniform system of laws, 
then a Charter Act, 1833 was passed. Lord Macaulay said, "We would like to have 
uniform laws for this country, but uniform only to the extent that it is possible. This is 
a country of diversity, and, a pluralistic society. We will not go into the personal law 
of Hindus and Muslims". This is recorded in the debates of Charter Act, 1833. So, 
from that time onwards, our country has be en governed by personal laws of all 
religious denominations.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Saraswati Heritage Project 
*61. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
CULTURE be pleased to state the progress made in the project on unearthing the 
Saraswati River Heritage Project? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): No sanction order 
in regard to Sarasvati Heritage Project was issued. The Project Report was prepared in 
September 2003 envisaging a cost of Rs. 36.02 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 
4.98 crores as reflected in the financial concurrence accorded on 01.03.2004. This 
amount was to be met from the regular budgetary provisions. 
In anticipation of sanction of the project, six sites were taken up for excavation in 
the year 2003-04, in addition to three sites which had been taken up earlier. The 
excavations are in progress. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY:  Sir, this is the most 
important project. Normally, there is a practice followed in our country that whenever a 
new Government assumes office, they will be undoing all the previous projects since they 
have their own priorities. But here is a project which the former Minister, Jagmohanji, has 
initiated, and he has done a lot of good work since it has got its own importance. Sir, the 
unearthing of the Sarasvati River route had a close link with the ancient Harappan 
civilisation. I would like to know from the hon. Minister the details of the sites excavated so 
far for exploration work, and the results achieved. 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, as I mentioned in my written answer, the then 
Government accorded financial sanction on 1st March, 2004 by which time the 
elections had been announced. The Re port as such was prepared only in 
September, 2003 envisaging a cost of Rs. 36.02 crores, which was reduced, in 
just three months, to Rs. 4.98 crores. In fact, no Sanction Order was issued. It 
all confined to files. But as I said, we were taking up excavations, six sites were 
taken up for excavation in 2003-04. Earlier, three sites has been taken up. 
Excavations on all the sites will be in progress, and they are in progress. Sir, 
all these sites, nine, are part of, what may be considered, Harappan Zone. Since 
Harappa and Mohanjodro are in Pakistan, we wanted to know as an independent 
India as to whether they were zones in our part of the country, and we did find, we 
did excavate Dholavera site, to a great extent. We found a lot of archaeological 
objects which were datable to pre-Harappan, Harappan historical periods. But, 
Sir, this has nothing to do with the Sarasvati River Project as such. These 
excavations will go on. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, my second 
supplementary is, whether several pre- Harappan sites have been found while 
exploring the roots of rivers and whethe r the Archaeological Survey of India 
would be asked to quicken the work on important heritage projects to build tourist 
hubs and develop the new places excavated for attracting tourists. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: First of all, Sir, as for tourist hub sites, this is a 
project taken up by the Tourism Ministry. At the time, Jagmohanji was 
handling both the Ministries. Therefore, I am afraid, I am not competent to answer 
the question. However, I said that the work was going on at all the nine sites 
because we want to know the facts. Nobody should hesitate to know the facts. 
Facts, in my view, are sacred. 
SHRI LEKHRAJ BACHANI: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether he knows that a very deep and extensive study was done by one 
Vedic scholar, Shri K.K. Sastri, of Ahmedabad. He is 100 years old. He has 
recently written a book on "Saraswati". He visited all the nine sites. He has also 
given some indications in his book. I would like to know from the hon. Minister 
whether he or his Department or his Ministry would make a study of the contents 
of that book and pursue the contents of that book. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, I have not read the book. The literature so far 
available does indicate that all these nine sites could be considered 
2 

[6 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
either pre-Harappan or Harappan or historical sites. They are all of high 
archaeological value. My only appeal to  the Members is not to confuse the 
archaeological value with a particular kind of project. 
DR. K. KASTURIRANGAN: Sir, I just want to bring, through you, to the 
attention of the hon. Minister that th e study from space revealed the existence 
of an ancient riverine system. Whether it is Sarawati or not, it is not important. The 
second component is that there are conjectures regarding the way it disappeared, 
including the violent plate tectonic movements in that region. The third 
component is hydrology, the potential of water, in case the riverine system had 
contributed to the subterranean ducts. Last one, of course, is archaeology. Any 
study which is related to the archaeological site excavation should also be 
suplemented and complemented by the other disciplines and it could be a very nice 
integrated study of that region from several of these disciplines point of view. I 
would request the hon. Minister to consider it as a proposal. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: I think it is a good suggestion. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, I take all the facts mentioned by the hon. 
Member, who is one of our eminent scientists, very seriously. We will think 
of an inter-discjplinary study. At the moment, we are engaged in excavations. 
As and when the facts of excavation warrant such a study, we will not hesitate 
to take up such a study. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Hon. Chairman, Sir, may I ask, through you, the 
hon. Minister whether the procedure, as I understand it, of finalising sites for 
excavation is on the basis of proposals from certain stipulated organisations like 
Universities, State Governments and academic bodies? Then there is the Central 
Advisory Board which advises the Archaeological Survey of India on the 
excavation. I would like to know from the hon. Minister as to who mooted the 
original proposal for the so-called Saraswati River Project to which the question 
refers. What was the date on which the Central Advisory Board came to this 
conclusion that these were the sites which were to be excavated? 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, the then Minister took some initiative in the 
matter in December, 2002, if I recall correctly. I don't have those dates with me. 
Later, it was referred to the Central Advisory Board of Archaeologists. They also 
cleared it. Even otherwise, we are guided by the advice of this Board. I am trying 
to differentiate excavation from the speci fic project. As and when the data 
thrown up warrants such a project, I will certainly commission the project. At 
the moment, I do not find any need for it. 
3 

RAJYA  SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, the Minister has not answered my question. I want the 
specific name of the body which proposed it and on the basis of which the Central Advisory 
Board took cognizance of that proposal. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: The Minister, at that time, formed a Committee with himself as 
the Chairperson for this purpose and took a view on the file; while no decision 
materialised in the form of sanction. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: The disappearance of the River Saraswati is one of the great 
mysteries of our archaeology and of our history because from the Sangam, the Ganga, the 
Yamuna and the Saraswati, W&R\ ST^T^I M % I Where did it go? How did it go? The 
Minsiter has said that it is only after the excavation that he would consider an integrated 
project as suggested by one of the hon. Members. My submission is this. Wouldn't the 
Minister like to do the two things simultaneously? You can do remote sensing, you can do 
satellite photography and you can also do excavations so that if there is a link between the 
disappeared river and the archaeological sites, that can be found. They don't have to come 
seriatim, perhaps they can go contiguously. 
SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY: Sir, the suggestion will be studied. But as of now, we have 
only found archaeological objects whose dates can be traced to pre-Harappa and Harappa culture. 
There are certain rivulets now. Beyond that there is not enough evidence to show that a particular 
river had existed in the past.

number of schemes have been formulated by the Central Government for development

education all over the country. The scheme gives special focus for the education of girls, 
scheduled castes and tribal children. The scheme also seeks to provide at least a 1:40

Support for Primary Education (commonly known as the Mid-day Meal Scheme) has

Secondary levels, Kendriya and Navodaya Vidyalayas have been set up in different parts of

Statement 
National Policy for Senior Citizens 
In pursuance to the National Policy on Older Persons, the Government has set 
up a National Council for Older Persons (NCOP) under the Chairmanship of 
Minister (SJ&E) in 1999. The NCOP is broad-based to advise and coordinate 
with the Government in the formulation and implementation of National Policy 
and programmes for the welfare of the aged. The Council also works as a nodal 
point at the national level for redressing the grievances of older persons and to 
represent their collective opinion to the Government 
Besides, the Ministry has also set up an Inter Ministerial Committee (IMC) 
headed by Secretary (SJ&E) with the sole aim of effective implementation of 
the National Policy on Older Persons and for taking action on the 
recommendations of NCOP. The Ministry periodically reviews progress on the 
implementation of the National Policy on Older Persons through meetings of 
NCOP and IMC. The last meeting of the IMC was held on 30.11.2004. 
Some of the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India concerned 
with the welfare of senior citizens are extending various facilities/ concessions for 
the welfare of older persons which are as under: 
Financial Security 
Income Tax rebate of upto Rs. 20,000 or actual tax whichever is less is allowed 
to senior citizens who have attained the age of 65 years, thereby exempting 
annual income upto Rs. 1.53 lakh from income tax. 
For Senior Citizens, deduction in respect of medical insurance premia upto 
Rs. 15,000/- is allowed while calculating the taxable income. 
A Special Senior Citizens Savings Scheme with provision of higher 
interest. 
45

Under the Old Age Pension Scheme, monthly pension is given at variable rates to 
the destitute old. The number of persons covered under the scheme during 2001-02 
was around 54.30 lakh,. 
Health Security 
Medical insurance like Mediclaim Policy is available for senior citizens up to 
75 years of age Universal Health Insurance Scheme for senior citizens upto 75 
years of age. 
Separate queues for older persons in hos pitals for registration and cilinical 
examination. 
Evening OPDs for the elderly in some government hospitals. 
Development of training module for doctors in the care of the elderly. 
Food Security 
Antyodaya Scheme: 2 crore families from amongst those with income below 
the poverty line have been covered under the Targeted Public Distribution 
System. 35 kg of food grains are provided  to each eligible family at a highly 
subsidized rate. The elderly members of such families benefit from this 
assistance. 
Annapoorna Scheme: 10 kgs. of food grains per person per month is 
provided free of cost to those senior citizens who remain uncovered under 
the old age pension scheme.  
Concessions in travel 
Reservation of two seats for senior citizens in front row of the public buses. 
Indian Railways provide 30% fare concession in all trains for senior 
citizens aged 60 years and above. 
50 per cent Senior Citizens discount on air fares subject to certain 
conditions. 
Separate counters for Senior Citizens for purchase/booking/cancellation of 
tickets. 
Other provisions 
Cells for redressal of grievances of the elderly in government departments. Early 
hearing of court cases involving older persons. 
46

Financial assistance is provided to Non Governmental Organisations for 
construction and maintenance of old age homes, day care centres and mobile 
medicare units by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. 
Legal provisions for protection of older persons from physical and 
emotional abuse and domestic violence. 
A rebate of 30% of the tax due on the covered space of such building up to one 
hundred sq. mtrs. of the covered space has been allowed by the Municipal 
Corporation of Delhi in the case of any self-occupied residential building singly 
owned by a man who is sixty years or more in age. 
Under Section 125 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 every person having 
sufficient means is required to maintain the parents if they are unable to 
maintain themselves. 
The Ministry has requested all State Governments to frame their State Policy 
on Older Persons. So far, the State Governments of Karnataka and Goa have 
already announced their State Policy for Older Persons. 
Further as per the directions of this Ministry, the Director Generals of Police 
of most of the States and Union Territories have issued instructions to their field 
formations about special attention to be paid for safeguarding the lives and 
properties of senior citizens.

Quality standards for agricultural products 
306. SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the countries signatory to the World Trade Organisation's 
Agreement on Agriculture have prescribed specific quality and 
sanitary/phyto sanitary standards for different agricultural produce they 
import; 
(b) if so, whether these standards are uniform and identical for all the 
countries of origin; 
 
(c) what are the standards for the commodities exported by India; 
(d) what are the facilities, like testing laboratories, available to farmers in 
the country; 
(e) whether Government propose to extend and improve these testing 
facilities; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) Members of the 
World Trade Organization (WTO) have undertaken to subscribe to the 
Agreement establishing the WTO along with other annexed multilateral 
Agreements, including th e Agreement on Agricultu re and the Agreement on 
Sanitary and Phyto-Sanitary Measures  (SPS), in the form of a 'single 
undertaking'. As per the SPS Agreement,  Member countries are expected to 
harmonize their standards with international standards (Codex Alimentarius 
Commission for human health, International Plant Protection Convention 
(IPPC) for plant health and International Office of Epizootics (OIE) for 
animal health). The SPS Agreement, however, provid es that in case more 
stringent standards are applied by any country, these have to be based on 
scientific principles and risk analys is. Members shall ensure that their 
sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures do not arbitrarily or unjustifiably 
53 

RAJYA SABHA  [6 December, 2004] 
discriminate between members were identical or similar conditions prevail, 
including between their own territory and that of other members. Sanitary and 
phytosanitary measures shall not be applied in a manner which would constitute a 
disguised restriction on international trade. 
(c) Under the Export (Quality Control & Inspection) Act, 1963, at present there 
are 6 product groups that are covered under compulsory export quality control and 
inspection. These products include fish and fishery products, dairy products, egg 
products, poultry products, meat products and honey. Notifications have been brought out 
subjecting these products to mandatory quality control and inspection prior to 
export. The standards applicable have been generally laid down which inter alia 
include: (i) National standards of importing country, (ii) Contractual 
specifications agreed to between the foreign buyer and the exporters provided that 
the same satisfies the health and other requirements of the importing country and (iii) 
in the absence of these two, the minimum specifications laid down in the 
notifications, The standards broadly cover the physical and chemical parameters as 
well as residues for pesticides, veterinary drugs, heavy metals etc. which are 
specified in the notifications. 
(d) In order to improve the testing facilities, the Government of India have already 
set up/strengthened a Central Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (Izatnagar, Bareilly) 
and four Regional Disease Diagnostic Laboratories (Jallandhar, Pone, Bangalore and 
Kolkata). Ultra-modern Plant Quarantine Laboratory facilities are established at the 
five (5) major Plant Quarantine Stations (Amritsar, Chennai, Kolkata, Mumbai and 
New Delhi) for undertaking Quarantine inspection and testing of agricultural 
commodities either imported into or exported out of the country. 
(e) and (f) Yes, improvement of the testing laboratories and related facilities is a 
constant endeavour of the Government. It has been proposed, under, the Tenth 
Plan, to strengthen further Quarantine laboratory facilities for inspection of 
agricultural commodities at the other major/minor ports:

vulnerable sections of the domestic industry, the Framework Agreement 
provides for each country to maintain a negative/ sens itive list of items on 
which no tariff concessions shall be granted under the FTA. In addition, the 
Agreement provides for trade defence measures which an importing country 
can take recourse to. In case of a surge in imports and injury to the domestic 
industry, a country is allowed to take measures such as anti-dumping and 
safeguards. The Agreement also provides for cooperation among customs 
authorities for ensuring that the Rules are not violated.

Non-tariff barriers on agricultural exports 
326. SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a)' whether it is a fact that the countries signatory to the Agreement on Agriculture 
under the World Trade Organisation (WTO) have prescribed different kinds of non-tariff 
barriers with a view to restricting their imports into their territories; and 
(b) if so, the details of the non-tariff barriers prescribed by the countries importing 
agricultural produce from India in respect of these commodities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 
(SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) The Most Favoured Nation (MFN) Treatment 
requirement of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) does not permit any 
discrimination or restriction specific to Indian goods by other WTO Members. Moreover, 
WTO rules allow restrictions on imports of goods based on tariffs as agreed upon and also 
through specific non-tariff measures, including those based on balance of payment grounds, 
sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures, conformity with agreed/international standards and 
contingent protection measures like anti-dumping, subsidy and safeguard actions. 
Nevertheless, non-tariff barriers, beyond agreed WTO rules, exist on import of goods 
from India in some WTO Member countries, including maintenance of sanitary and 
phyto-sanitary measurs at levels which are not readily justifiable on the basis of 
scientific evidence. Procedural requirements could also act as barriers to trade. Problems 
arising due to non-tariff barriers are duly taken up by Government with the concerned 
authorities of the country concerned either bilaterally with a view to their early and 
mutually satisfactory resolution or presented for resolution by the WTO's Dispute 
Settlement Mechanism. In the ongoing W TO negotiations, India has also co-sponsored 
proposals alongwith some other developing countries to disallow use of measures by 
developed countries that act as barriers to imports from developing countries.

340. SHRI R.P GOENKA: Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the UNESCO has proposed to classify some of the 
world heritage sites in India, including Hampi in Karnataka, in the "endangered" 
category; and

UN agency and the steps being taken to preserve the integrity, of the archaeological 
sites by saving them from any physical harm or compromising their unique ambience 
and scenic surroundings? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The World Heritage Committee has placed two World Heritage sites-the 
Group of Monuments at Hampi and the Manas Wild Life Sanctuary-in the 
endangered category. As far as the archaeological site of Hampi is concerned, it was 
put in list of danger in 1999 due to construction of a bridge across the river 
Tungabhadra in the core zone area of the site. Two UNESCO Missions have visited 
the site and suggested corrective measures. The important suggestions are: 
(a) to construct a road by passing the core zone 
(b) to prepare a comprehensive site management plan 
(c) to include local communities in the development programmes envisaged at 
the site etc. 
The Government of Karnataka has taken steps to construct the new By-pass road by 
acquiring requisite land and the work is in progress. School of Planning and 
Architecture, New Delhi is entrusted with the work of formulating comprehensive 
site management plan to address

various issues relating to development and to maintain the integrity and authenticity of 
the World Heritage Site.

making all. efforts to implement the recommendations and corrective measures suggested 
by the World Heritage Committee. 
Manas Wild Life Sanctuary was put in danger list in 1992. The World Heritage Centre 
approved a rehabilitation plan and agreed to provide, international assistance. The World 
Heritage Committee in its 28th session recommended: 
(i)  to undertake a mission to assess the security situation and ecological 
conditions 
(ii)  to begin activities benefiting the site as soon as possible.

375. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE

(b) if so, the details thereof; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (c) Transfers made under 
the guidelines with effect from April 1,2000 in the Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan 
(KVS) led to a widespread dislocation of teachers across the country. Many of them 
were transferred thousands of kilometers away from their place of residence and 
families. Many couples were also separated across thousands of kilometers. This 
caused widespread misery in the entire system. Hundreds of teachers resigned from the 
service, some were dismissed for their inability to join in remote places. The measure not 
only affected families but also deprived KVS of experienced teachers. The recent transfer

to their places of residence. The salient features of modified transfer guidelines are 
as under:— 
(i)   The concept of "displacement transfers" has been done away with. 
(ii)   The transfers should mostly be done only against vacancies on the basis of 
requests received for the same. 
(iii)  In general, teachers/staff members will not be transferred except on 
administrative grounds. 
(iv)   The concept of surplus teachers has been changed from the existing criteria 
of declaring the teachers with longest stay as surplus to the teachers with 
least number of years served in a particular Vidyalaya. 
(v)   In order to ensure that there is minimum disruption of teachers from 
Kendriya Vidyalayas, it has been decided that even in case of promotion 
of teachers, the teachers can continue to work in the same Vidyalaya 
provided there is a vacancy. In case there is no vacancy he/she can exercise 
his request for the nearest available vacancies. 
(vi)   In order to provide relief to teachers who resigns from the service or were 
dismissed following their inability to join in places of posting as a result of 
transfer guidelines of the year 2000, a Committee has been constituted to 
consider the appeals of such teachers. They can appeal before this 
committee latest by 15th December, 2004 and this committee would take 
a decision within a month after that. This humane approach in the current 
transfer policy has been widely appreciated and it is hoped that within a 
year or two the KVS will be able to redress the grievances, of all the 
affected teachers to a substantial extent.

Vulgarity on Cable TV and print media 
389. SHRIMATIPREMACARIAPPA: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have devised any action plan or code of conduct for checking 
vulgarity on cable TV network and print media; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) and (b) The Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 prescribe that 
no programme shall be carried through Cable TV Network, provided it conforms to the 
Programme and Advertisement Codes as defined in the Cable Television Networks Rules, 
1994. The Programme and Advertisement Codes cited, inter alia, prohibit vulgarity through 
cable T.V. network. The Central Government has constituted an Inter-Ministerial 
Committee under Section 20 of the said Act to look into the violations of the Codes. 
Cognizance of any violations of the Codes is taken either suo-moto or on receipt of specific 
complaints by the Committee. Besides, any authorized officer under the aforesaid Act is 
empowered to prohibit any cable operator from transmitting or re-transmitting any 
programme or channel if it is not in conformity with the prescribed codes. A meeting is 
also proposed to be held shortly with stakeholders including women organizations, 
educations, consumer organisation with broadcasters, cable operators organisation etc., so that 
the matter can be sensitized on these issues. 
As regards print media, the Press in India is free from Government control. In 
pursuance of its policy to uphold the freedom of the Press, the Government does not 
interfere with its functioning. However, the Press Council of India is a statutory 
autonomous body set up under the Press Council Act, 1978 with the twin object of 
preserving the freedom of the Press and of maintaining and improving the standards of 
newspapers and 
148 

[6 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
news agencies in India. The Council has built "Norms of Journalistic 
Conduct", which, inter-alia, provide for obsenity and vulgarity to be 
eschewed and cover principles and ethics with regard to journalism.

MATTER RAISED WITH PERMISSION OF CHAIR 
Re: Non-payment Of Access Deficit Charges (ADC) By Private Telecom 
Operators 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir, with a very heavy 
heart, I rise today to bring to the notice of the House and also the Government 
regarding the huge scam in the telecom sector that has been taking place for the 
last one year, or, maybe, even more. But, Sir, as somebody who has been 
associated with this House for creating a situation whereby universal telecom 
connectivity can be provided to the people of this country, I Find instances where 
institutions, which have been created through enactments by this august House, 
have criminally neglected their responsibility, in enforcing regulation and in due 
discharge of the legal powers that were provided to them. The result today, Sir, is 
that an amount of more than Rs. 2000 crores which was to be paid by certain 
private telecom operators to the Government and, through the Government, to the 
Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited, to provide telecom connectivity to backward rural 
areas, far-flung areas has not been paid. Sir, now it is common knowledge 
and it is part of the public domain that a prima facie case has been established in 
regard to non-payment of ADCs at the prescribed rates which were stipulated 
by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, and also through the order of the 
Government of India. Sir, the sordid story begins with having a telecom regulator 
that was pliant, that was close to the Government. I recall the proceedings of this 
House when initially we had created the TRAI; and many of the Members in the 
Government today were part of the process. 
Sir, in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of that Act, what we had 
provided for was that "TRAI will be set up for protection and promotion of 
consumer interest, and ensuring fair competition. There is a felt need to separate 
regulatory functions from service-providing functions, which will be in keeping with 
the general trend in the world." It further said, "in which the private operator will be 
competing with Government operators, there is a pressing need for an independent 
telecom regulatory body for regulation 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2004] 
of telecom services for orderly and healthy growth of telecommunication 
infrastructure, apart from protection of consumer interest." 
Now, Sir, I refer to the order of the Telecom Regulatory Authority that for every 
international call, the operators that were bringing in the international calls were 
supposed to pay Rs. 4.25 to the Government, which goes to the BSNL for 
providing telecom connectivity. Sir, the two consultation papers of the Telecom 
Regulatory Authority show — I do not, for the paucity of time, go into the specific 
orders; I have them with me — that this differential between access deficit charge, 
which was to be paid for national long distance calls and international long 
distance calls, created a situation whereby grey.market could emerge. The 
TRAI also, in the report of the Sub-Committee that it created, where it included 
representatives of the Government, of the public sector telecom operator as well as 
private sector companies, says that this a very serious situation and grey market 
has, indeed, emerged. 
Sir, the issue is not only non-payment of money; there is an element of national 
security also. This should be also taken note of by the hon. Finance Minister. Telecom 
today has security implications, and this has been noted by the Government of India 
in its order, which states that when the party is calling from a foreign land to our 
telephones, normally we should have the caller line identification appearing on our 
handsets. But they were tempered with by the private players to avoid paying the 
legitimate access deficit charges. Sir, I tested myself day before yesterday 
when I called some friend in England and I asked him to call back. I saw that 
there was no caller line identification still available on my handset. This is 15 days 
after the DoT has come out with a public advertisement in all Indian newspapers that 
when you see that there is no caller line identification appearing on your 
handsets, you shall understand that this is part of the whole imbroglio which leads to 
grey market and which leads to fleecing of public money. 
Now, I may say, Sir, that the appointment of the present regulator, present 
Chairman of the TRAI, has led to a decline in rural connectivity in terms of 
telecommunication in our country. I have the facts and figures with me. 
Actually, the telecom growth has led to tremendous inequities between the 
urban sector and the rural sector. Today, for every 1.6 telephones in the rural 
areas, there are 20 telephones in the urban areas, and the gap is widening; Sir, it is 
a shame that this is despite knowing that grey market will emerge. This is 
documented, in all these documents of TRAI consultation papers, as well as the 
Sub-Committee notes, and they

say that they pose a very grave threat, and recommend the stringent of 
punishments like cancellation of ILD licence, and proceeding against them in 
accordance with national security laws. 
Sir, we are the only Parliament which was attacked by the terrorists, and 
whatever we could do in terms of investigation was on the basis of the CLI which 
was available from the telephones of the extremist elements and the terrorist 
elements who attacked the Parliament. Now, there is a very serious 
security breach. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: That is enough. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, the Government of India, which had this

been fleeced; how much manipulation has taken place; and, who are 
responsible. Sir, as late as the 1st of December, the whole nation knew, through 
the Government's reply in the Lok Sabha, that the breach was only to the tune of 
Rs. 300 crores, whereas BSNL and MTNL, the two public sector telecom 
companies, have filed claims for about Rs. 600 crores. The Government is 
saying, "Only Rs. 300 crores", and this is a very serious issue. We are told; 
press reports are coming that the Ministry says that if they cancel the licence 
of all those private operators, the consumers will be affected which is a total 
untruth because in terms of inter national long distance operator licence

by the Government in public interest. This is a very serious issue. Secondly, 
the Government should institute a full-fledged inquiry into the whole scam which 
has led to fleecing money to the tune of more than Rs. 2000 crores which 
should have provided telephone coverage for the rural areas and far-flung areas 
which is the core commitment of the Common Minimum Programme. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Basu, that is enough. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, as a result of this, we want the most stringent

SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka): Sir, I would like to draw the

The Government had launched a national scheme for liberation and 
rehabilitation of scavengers and their dependents in 1992. An amount of Rs. 600 
crores was spent over 12 years but the scheme has failed to make any 
distinct improvement. Despite the existing law that prohibited employment of 
scavengers, many States are yet to enforce it in true letter and spirit.

amounting to Rs. 64.80 crores, belonged to this scheme. Thus, whatever funds 
were allocated for this scheme could not be utilized. I urge upon the Government to 
relaunch this scheme with more funds and ensure that the funds are fully utilized 
within the stipulated time-frame.
